title: Going cashless, and who gets left out

turns.speaker: Tomas
turns.text: Three places on my street now refuse cash outright. Not prefer card. Refuse.

turns.speaker: Zara
turns.text: It's cheaper for them. Counting it, banking it, the risk of holding it, all of that goes away.

turns.speaker: Beth
turns.text: And the people it shuts out are exactly who you'd expect. The very old, people without an address, anyone whose bank closed their account.

turns.speaker: Tomas
turns.text: How many is that, realistically? Because it feels like a shrinking problem.

turns.speaker: Beth
turns.text: Around one adult in fifty relies on cash for most of what they buy. It is shrinking. It isn't nothing.

turns.speaker: Zara
turns.text: The bit that worries me more is resilience. When the card network went down last winter, the cash shops kept trading and the others shut.

turns.speaker: Tomas
turns.text: That's a good point and it's not the one people usually make.

turns.speaker: Beth
turns.text: There's a budgeting argument too. Physical money is visibly finite in a way a contactless card isn't, and the people who most need that are the ones being pushed off it.

turns.speaker: Zara
turns.text: Which is measurable, I think. People do spend more on card for the same basket.

turns.speaker: Tomas
turns.text: So what's the actual ask? You can't force a coffee shop to take coins.

turns.speaker: Beth
turns.text: Sweden decided you can, roughly. Essential services have to accept it. Not every shop, but the pharmacy and the bus.

turns.speaker: Zara
turns.text: That seems proportionate. It's the difference between inconvenience and exclusion.

points: Several local businesses now refuse cash entirely, because handling it costs them money.
Beth notes the excluded groups: the very old, people without an address, and those refused bank accounts, about one adult in fifty.
Zara raises resilience, since cash-accepting shops kept trading during a card network outage.
Beth adds a budgeting argument, that physical money is visibly finite in a way contactless payment is not, and people spend more on card for the same basket.
Tomas questions what can be required of a private business.
They settle on the Swedish approach of obliging essential services such as pharmacies and buses to accept cash, distinguishing inconvenience from exclusion.
